AI Adoption Pilot Studies — proposals for extending AI beyond current production systems, one per adoption pillar
PREDICTIVE MAINTENANCE
Precision Machining Pilot — TBD
4–8 week pilot · Single CNC machining cell · NexGen Predict
Phase 2 — Pilot Proposal

Executive Summary
TBD machines precision, safety-critical components for major automotive OEMs including GM, Ford, Honda, Toyota, and Tesla. These customers hold suppliers to IATF 16949 quality standards, just-in-time delivery windows, and zero tolerance for late or defective shipments — making an unplanned machine failure a direct threat to on-time delivery and future sourcing decisions.

This pilot proposes a focused predictive maintenance program on a single CNC machining cell, using Corverxis NexGen Predict, to demonstrate that IoT-sensor-driven failure prediction can give the maintenance team 24+ hours of advance warning before a bearing, spindle, or servo failure — replacing reactive "firefighting" with planned intervention.

A narrow, well-instrumented pilot is the fastest path to organizational trust: once the floor sees NexGen Predict catch a real failure before it happens, they become the strongest internal advocates for extending AI adoption to quality inspection, supply chain planning, and process optimization.
Industry Context
Siemens (2024): unplanned downtime at large automotive plants runs up to $2.3M/hour — roughly $600/second.
Aberdeen Research: cross-industry manufacturing average is closer to $260K/hour — automotive runs far steeper.
Industry surveys of automotive execs: stoppage costs of $22K–$50K/minute once idled labor, expedited parts, and shipment penalties are included.
Why Predictive Maintenance Is the Right First Pilot
1. Immediate Value
A prevented crash is a visible, dateable win — not an abstract statistic.
2. Builds Trust
Maintenance techs are the most skeptical audience — and once convinced, the most credible advocates.
3. Low Friction
Layers onto existing maintenance workflow — no change to how parts are actually made.
4. Data Foundation
IIoT + MES integration built here is a prerequisite for Vision QC, Supply Chain AI, and Process Optimization.
Recommended Pilot Scope
DimensionScope
LocationOne CNC cell — high-tolerance safety-critical part
Assets1–3 machines, incl. one with known failure history
SensorsVibration · Temperature · Acoustic · Current draw
Duration4–8 weeks end to end
TeamMaintenance lead, 2–3 operators, 1–2 technicians, Corverxis engineer
Implementation Timeline
WeekPhaseFocus
1–2Data FoundationSensor install, baseline capture, threshold calibration
3–4Pilot — LiveLive RUL monitoring begins; operator training via CorverxisAcademy
5–6Pilot — LiveContinued monitoring; log every alert and outcome
7Results ReviewCompile downtime avoided, technician hours saved
8Decision PointRecommend Phase 3 (Scaling) scope

Illustrative Business Case
Industry-benchmark illustrations, not a guarantee for any specific facility.
• One averted 30–60 min stoppage can exceed the entire pilot's cost, based on reported automotive downtime of $22K–$50K/minute.
• Deloitte: predictive maintenance programs typically reduce breakdowns ~70% vs. reactive/preventive baselines.
• Industry benchmarks commonly report 25–40% maintenance cost reduction under mature PdM programs.
Key Risks & Mitigations
• Limited history → confidence scores shown transparently; improve as data accumulates
• False positives → tracked explicitly as a pilot KPI, tuned weekly
• Floor skepticism → addressed directly via Change Management comms, not deferred
Path to Scale
A successful pilot supports two scaling tracks: horizontal — extending predictive maintenance to additional CNC cells using the validated sensor/alerting architecture — and vertical — applying the trust and data foundation built here to the next AI adoption pillars already defined in the roadmap: computer-vision quality inspection, AI-assisted supply and inventory planning, and process (Golden Batch) optimization. The pilot's greatest asset isn't the technology validation — it's a floor team that has personally seen the system prevent a real problem.
Sources: Siemens True Cost of Downtime research (2024) · Aberdeen Research manufacturing downtime benchmarking · Deloitte Analytics Institute predictive maintenance position paper · industry surveys of automotive manufacturing executives on production stoppage costs. Figures are directional industry benchmarks; the pilot itself is designed to produce facility-specific results for TBD.

Executive Summary
TBD supplies safety-critical precision components to automotive OEMs who require 100% inspection coverage on key characteristics — not statistical sampling. Manual visual inspection has a well-documented accuracy ceiling: peer-reviewed research places typical industry accuracy around 80%, and a widely cited MIT study found human inspectors maintain a 70–85% defect detection rate before fatigue-driven error sets in.

This pilot proposes Corverxis Vision — AI-powered optical inspection — on a single inspection station, running in parallel with the existing manual process, to demonstrate a direct, measurable accuracy comparison before any inspection responsibility is handed over.

Every AI-flagged part below the confidence threshold routes to a human review queue — the pilot is designed to remove the fatigue-driven error rate from the large majority of clear calls, not replace the inspector's judgment on genuinely uncertain ones.
Industry Context
PMC/NCBI (2023): typical manual visual inspection accuracy runs ~80% across industry — a documented, not anecdotal, ceiling.
MIT-cited research: human inspectors average 70–85% detection; AI vision systems consistently exceed 95%.
Industry analyses citing McKinsey: AI vision improves detection rates up to 90% while cutting inspection costs 50%+.
Why Computer Vision QC Is a High-Value Pilot
1. Closes a Known Gap
80–85% manual ceiling vs. 95%+ AI accuracy — large enough to matter and to prove in a short pilot.
2. No Process Change
Adds inspection capability — doesn't touch machining parameters or tooling.
3. IATF-Ready Evidence
Every decision + confidence score is logged — exactly the traceable record IATF 16949 audits look for.

LocationOne inspection station, highest-defect-cost part
Coverage100% of parts — not a sampling rate
DefectsCracks, porosity, dimensional deviation, finish
Duration4–6 weeks, incl. parallel run vs. manual
TeamQE lead, 1–2 inspectors, Corverxis engineer
Implementation Timeline

Illustrative Business Case
Industry-benchmark illustrations, not a guarantee for any specific facility.
• AI vision can improve defect detection up to 90% vs. manual baseline (industry analyses citing McKinsey).
• Inspection labor cost reductions of 50%+ once AI handles the high-confidence majority.
• A 1% defect rate reaching customers in high-volume automotive can cost millions once recalls/scorecarding are included.
Key Risks & Mitigations
• Lighting/camera drift → daily calibration + mid-shift recheck
• High false-positive rate → tracked explicitly, tuned weekly
• Inspector role concern → staffed into review-queue role from day one
Path to Scale
A successful pilot supports two tracks: horizontal — extending Corverxis Vision to additional inspection stations and defect types — and vertical — tighter integration with the NCR and corrective-action workflow already in CorverxisONE. The pilot's most durable outcome is a quality team that has personally verified the AI system's judgment against their own, station by station.

Executive Summary
TBD sources specialty steel, aluminum, and precision-grade raw materials to meet just-in-time delivery windows set by automotive OEM customers. A stockout on a critical material stops production; excess inventory ties up working capital. Both are direct, measurable costs of forecast error.

This pilot proposes Corverxis Supply Chain AI — AI-assisted demand forecasting and reorder-point optimization — on one high-criticality material category, to demonstrate a measurable reduction in forecast error and the safety stock required to protect against it.

Every AI-suggested reorder point is a recommendation the buyer confirms or overrides — overrides and reasons are logged explicitly, since that context is exactly what the model can't see on its own.
Industry Context
E2open Benchmark Study (2021, 2024): AI + real-time demand sensing cut forecast error by 32–36%, based on real operational data.
DP World / Supply Chain Dive (2025): AI adopters report up to 50% fewer forecast errors, 65% fewer lost sales.
KPMG: each 1-point forecast accuracy gain → 1–2% drop in inventory levels.
Why AI-Assisted Supply Chain Is a High-Value Pilot
1. Directly Calculable Cost
A stockout or overstock has a directly quantifiable dollar cost — easy to measure pilot success against.
2. Strengthens Buyer Judgment
The forecast is a recommendation the buyer confirms or overrides — augments, doesn't replace, purchasing judgment.
3. Existing Data, Fast Start
Builds on existing ERP/MES purchase history — useful signal from day one, no new sensor infrastructure.

• DP World: up to 65% fewer lost sales among AI-forecasting adopters.
Key Risks & Mitigations

Path to Scale
A successful pilot supports two tracks: horizontal — extending AI-assisted forecasting to additional material categories, prioritized by criticality — and vertical — using override-reason data to refine the model's handling of TBD-specific patterns a generic model wouldn't know. The pilot's most durable outcome is a buying team that trusts the forecast as a genuine second opinion, not a black box.

Executive Summary
Every CNC machining operation at TBD has dozens of adjustable parameters — spindle speed, feed rate, coolant pressure, dwell time. Experienced operators develop real intuition for "good" settings, but that intuition is hard to transfer, hard to prove optimal, and slow to update.

This pilot proposes Corverxis Golden Batch Analytics — AI analysis of historical MES data — on one CNC cell and part number with known scrap-rate variability, to identify the parameter combination that most consistently minimizes scrap, cycle time, and tool wear together, validated through a controlled floor trial.

A directly relevant precedent: a documented Lean Six Sigma DMAIC case study on an automotive-sensor sub-process improved First Run Yield from 98.4% to 99.03% — the same discipline of measuring before acting that underlies this pilot.
Industry Context
Documented DMAIC case study (airbag sensor "Overmould line"): First Run Yield 98.4% → 99.03%, Sigma 3.65 → 3.85.
AI-driven analysis reviews far more historical parameter-outcome combinations than a manual DMAIC study can practically cover by hand.
Core discipline is unchanged: measure with real data, find true root cause, test, then monitor — AI extends reach, doesn't replace the method.
Why Process Optimization Is a High-Value Pilot
1. Data Already Exists
Draws on historical MES work-order data already being captured — no new sensor infrastructure.
2. Directly Measurable
Judged against scrap rate, cycle time, tool life — metrics the floor already tracks.
3. Reinforces Expertise
AI surfaces candidates; operator judgment still validates every real trial run.
Recommended Pilot Scope
DimensionScope

Data6–12 months historical MES work orders
Duration5–7 weeks incl. controlled trial
TeamProcess engineer, 1–2 operators, Corverxis engineer

Illustrative Business Case
Based on a specific documented case study, not a guarantee for any other facility.
• Documented DMAIC case: FRY 98.4% → 99.03% on a comparable automotive-component sub-process.
• Even a fraction-of-a-percent scrap reduction is meaningful at automotive production volume.
• A "fast" setting that increases tool wear isn't optimal once tooling cost is included — the multi-metric evaluation Golden Batch performs.
Key Risks & Mitigations
• Incomplete MES data → dedicated validation phase before any candidate is surfaced
• Trial doesn't match prediction → investigated for root cause (tooling/material lot), not dismissed
• Operator skepticism → operators define what the trial validates, not told the result after the fact
Path to Scale
A successful pilot supports two tracks: horizontal — extending Golden Batch analysis to additional part numbers with documented variability — and vertical — feeding validated trial data back into a model that gets more accurate as more part numbers contribute real floor-validation results. The pilot's most durable outcome is a process team that has seen a data-surfaced recommendation hold up under real floor validation.
